lead: This unit introduces the basics of regular languages and the machines that recognise them. After reading, the student can model a language with a DFA, convert between different automata, minimise machines and understand output‑producing variants.
about: Unit 1 is divided into nine short chapters. Chapter 1.1 defines alphabets, strings and formal languages. Chapter 1.2 gives the formal definition of a deterministic finite automaton (DFA). Chapter 1.3 shows how to draw transition diagrams, build tables and use the extended transition function. Chapter 1.4 introduces nondeterministic finite automata (NFA). Chapter 1.5 adds ε‑moves to NFA. Chapter 1.6 proves DFA–NFA equivalence by the subset construction. Chapter 1.7 minimises DFA with the table‑filling algorithm. Chapter 1.8 presents Moore and Mealy machines. Chapter 1.9 (advanced) sketches two‑way finite automata. Each chapter builds on the previous one, preparing the student for regular expressions and later grammar topics.

chapters.idea: Define alphabet, string and language with precise notation.
chapters.depth: Cover symbols, length, concatenation, Kleene star, and common operations. Mention other names such as symbol set or vocabulary used in some syllabi.

figure.aria: Shows the alphabet Σ and a sample language L built from it.

chapters.example: Alphabet Σ={0,1}. List all strings of length ≤2: ε, 0, 1, 00, 01, 10, 11.
chapters.trap: Confusing string length with the number of strings in a language.
chapters.leave: Regular expressions and closure properties are covered in later units.

chapters.idea: Give the formal definition of a deterministic finite automaton.
chapters.depth: Explain states, start state, accept states, transition function δ: Q×Σ→Q. Use names DFA, deterministic finite‑state machine as seen in some syllabi.

figure.aria: State diagram of DFA that accepts strings ending in 01.

chapters.example: Design a DFA over Σ={0,1} that accepts all strings whose last two symbols are 01.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that δ must be defined for every state‑symbol pair.
chapters.leave: Transition tables and extended function are detailed in the next chapter.

chapters.idea: Show how to represent automata with diagrams, tables and the extended transition function.
chapters.depth: Build a transition diagram, a transition table, and define δ̂ that processes whole strings. Mention that some syllabi call this the extended transition function.

figure.aria: Shows the steps of the extended transition function on an input string.

chapters.example: Using the DFA from chapter 2, compute δ̂(q0, 1101) step by step and decide acceptance.
chapters.trap: Applying symbols in reverse order when using δ̂.
chapters.leave: NFA concepts are introduced in the next chapter.

chapters.idea: Define nondeterministic finite automata and their acceptance condition.
chapters.depth: Explain that δ returns a set of states, that multiple moves may exist, and a string is accepted if any computation ends in an accept state. Some syllabi refer to this as NFA or nondet finite‑state machine.

figure.aria: NFA graph where state p can go to q or r on symbol 0.

chapters.example: Construct an NFA that accepts any string containing the substring 101 over Σ={0,1}. Show a computation tree for input 110101.
chapters.trap: Assuming every possible path must accept; only one accepting path is needed.
chapters.leave: ε‑moves are added in the next chapter.

chapters.idea: Introduce ε‑moves and ε‑closure in finite automata.
chapters.depth: Define ε‑transition, ε‑closure of a state, and how to incorporate ε‑moves in the extended transition function. Some syllabi list this as ε‑NFA or NFA with ε‑moves.

figure.aria: ε‑NFA showing an ε‑move from s to t before reading input.

chapters.example: Design an ε‑NFA that accepts strings with an even number of 0s. Compute ε‑closure before reading each symbol for input 010.
chapters.trap: Skipping ε‑closure after a move, which may miss reachable states.
chapters.leave: Conversion to DFA using subset construction follows next.

chapters.idea: Convert any NFA (with or without ε‑moves) to an equivalent DFA by subset construction.
chapters.depth: Explain the algorithm: start state = ε‑closure(start), transition on a symbol = ε‑closure(move). Create a DFA state for each new subset. Some syllabi call this DFA–NFA equivalence.

figure.aria: Subset construction where DFA states are sets of NFA states.

chapters.example: Apply subset construction to the NFA of chapter 4. Show the DFA states {p}, {q,r}, and ∅, and list the resulting transition table.
chapters.trap: Omitting the empty set as a DFA state, which leads to incomplete tables.
chapters.leave: Minimisation of the resulting DFA is covered next.

chapters.idea: Merge indistinguishable DFA states using the table‑filling algorithm.
chapters.depth: Create a table of all unordered state pairs. Mark pairs with one accept and one reject. Propagate markings until no new pairs are marked. Remaining unmarked pairs form equivalence classes. Some syllabi refer to this as DFA minimisation.

figure.title: Distinguishable pairs
figure.aria: Table showing which state pairs are marked as distinguishable.

chapters.example: Minimise the DFA from chapter 2. Mark pair (q0,q2) as distinguishable, then derive the reduced DFA with two states.
chapters.trap: Failing to initially mark pairs where one state is accepting and the other is not.
chapters.leave: Output machines (Moore/Mealy) are introduced after minimisation.

chapters.idea: Define Moore and Mealy machines – finite automata that produce output.
chapters.depth: Moore machine: output attached to states. Mealy machine: output attached to transitions. Show conversion between the two. Some syllabi list these as finite‑state transducers.

figure.aria: Graph showing a Mealy machine (output on edges) and a Moore machine (output on states).

chapters.example: Design a Mealy machine that prints ‘Success’ (1) when a UPI transaction ID ends with 0 and ‘Fail’ (0) otherwise. Show the output for input 1010.
chapters.trap: Confusing whether output is produced before or after the transition.
chapters.leave: Two‑way automata are covered as an advanced topic.

chapters.idea: Allow the read head to move left or right on the input tape – two‑way finite automata.
chapters.depth: Define the transition function δ: Q×Σ∪{⊢,⊣}→Q×{L,R}. Explain that the model recognises exactly the regular languages, so it does not increase computational power. Only a few universities teach this.

figure.aria: Sequence diagram of a two‑way automaton moving left and right on the tape.

chapters.example: Construct a two‑way automaton that accepts the palindrome 10101. Show the head moves for input 10101.
chapters.trap: Assuming the ability to move left gives power beyond regular languages.
